segments.text: 25 years ago, if you made a spreadsheet in Excel,
you probably saved it directly to your computer's hard drive.
If that drive failed and you hadn't made a backup,
your work was gone.
Today, using a modern tool,
you can close your laptop, pull out your phone,
and instantly open the exact same file.
So where does that file live while your devices are turned off?
It sits on a server.
When you hear the phrase, the cloud,
it really just means computers connected over the internet,
holding your files and running programs on your behalf.
Now, imagine you share that same spreadsheet with chat GPT,
and type a prompt asking,
why did my expenses jump in March?
Keeping a copy of your spreadsheet on a server
is a relatively simple job,
but when AI analyzes data and writes a custom answer,
it relies on complex mathematics.
Doing that math requires drastically more computing power
than simply storing a file.
We are used to digital tools feeling weightless and instant.
But generating an AI response
actually kicks off a massive invisible mathematical engine
right behind your own screen.
To write that answer,
AI processes text in chunks called tokens.
It represents every single token as a vector,
a long row of numbers capturing its baseline meaning.
As the model builds a sentence,
it constantly updates thousands of these numbers
to understand how each word relates to the surrounding ones.
This shows how fast the math adds up.
For one token, an AI runs roughly 100 billion calculations.
To write a short answer, the total jumps to 10 trillion.
Over a longer conversation, it crosses 100 trillion calculations.
Even a brief sentence requires trillions of mathematical operations.
A casual question typed on your phone
triggers an astronomical chain reaction of math.
That sheer volume of processing is physically impossible
to run on a personal device.
The ability to execute all of that complex math
is known in the industry as compute.
That's the compute required for one person.
Now imagine millions of people asking their own unique questions
at the exact same moment.
Where does all that centralized math actually happen?
It takes place inside an AI data center.
A data center is a massive building packed with computers
called servers.
Inside an AI facility, these servers rely on specialized chips
called GPUs, graphics processing units,
that are built specifically to perform thousands of calculations
in parallel.
The physical footprint of these buildings is immense.
The biggest AI data centers cover the ground of multiple football fields
and draw as much electricity as a small city.
Inside one of these facilities, notice the person walking down the aisle,
dwarfed by the hardware.
These tall black cabinets are server racks stacked top to bottom housing GPUs.
To meet global compute demand, these rows repeat as far as the eye can see,
creating a dense grid of processing.
The ethereal cloud, we imagine, is actually a colossal,
energy-hungry physical factory operating quietly in the real world.
All that machinery requires vast amounts of local resources to run.
So what does a facility of this size mean for the people who actually live nearby?
This chart breaks down the physical toll of a data center
into four distinct impacts on a local neighborhood.
First is electricity.
Berkeley Lab estimates that by 2030, data centers could consume
about 12% of all U.S. electricity.
In some regions, this massive, added strain on the grid
is already raising household utility bills.
Next is water.
Processing chips run incredibly hot,
and cooling a large data center can require roughly a million gallons on a warm day.
Even advanced systems that recycle their coolant
continually need fresh water to replace what naturally evaporates.
Third is noise.
Massive cooling fans have to run 24 hours a day
to prevent the servers from melting down.
In some towns, neighbors have sued over the constant industrial hum and lost sleep.
Finally, permanent jobs.
While it takes a very large construction crew to build a data center,
far fewer people are actually employed to work inside once the facility officially opens.
The frictionless convenience of generating AI answers
comes at a direct physical cost to local resources,
electrical grids, and nearby communities.
The tech industry is taking steps to address these bottlenecks.
AI companies are aggressively negotiating to secure more electricity contracts
to keep their servers online.
Many operators are also shifting toward facilities that heavily reuse water
in their cooling systems to mitigate the impact on local drought conditions.
Meanwhile, hardware manufacturers are designing newer generations of chips
that can perform the same heavy mathematics using significantly less power.
This graphic is a final reminder of our digital footprint.
Behind every instantly generated answer on your screen,
there is a massive physical data center working in Overdrive.
And for someone else, that facility is part of their neighborhood.
